subject: religious-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which view is sometimes used to support capital punishment?
options: That it provides retribution and may deter the most serious crimes
questions.explain: Supporters argue capital punishment delivers proportionate retribution and may deter serious crime, though this is contested.

questions.q: What is 'corporal punishment'?
options: Punishment involving physical pain, such as caning
A fine paid to the court
questions.explain: Corporal punishment is physical punishment, such as caning, now banned in UK schools and prisons.

questions.q: Which of these is an aim of punishment?
options: Deterrence - discouraging others from committing crime
questions.explain: Deterrence aims to put people off committing crime through the threat of punishment.

questions.q: Why might a religious believer emphasise forgiveness towards a criminal?
options: Because crime should never have consequences
Because their faith teaches mercy and the chance to start again
questions.explain: Many faiths teach forgiveness and mercy alongside, not instead of, appropriate justice.

questions.q: A common misconception about the aims of punishment is that:
options: Punishment can serve several aims at once
Punishment must only ever serve one single aim
Deterrence and reformation can both apply
questions.explain: In practice, a punishment can combine several aims such as deterrence, protection and reformation.

questions.q: How do many religions teach believers to treat lawbreakers?
options: With justice but also compassion and the hope of forgiveness
questions.explain: Many faiths combine a call for justice with compassion, forgiveness and the possibility of change.

questions.q: What does the term 'recidivism' refer to?
options: The first crime a person ever commits
The release of an innocent person
When a released offender reoffends and returns to crime
questions.explain: Recidivism is reoffending; reducing it is a key aim of rehabilitation and reform.

questions.q: Which is a reason some religious believers support the rehabilitation of offenders?
options: They believe in the possibility of repentance and a fresh start
They believe offenders can never change
questions.explain: Many believers support rehabilitation because their faith teaches repentance and the chance to start again.

questions.q: What does 'reformation' as an aim of punishment focus on?
options: Helping the offender to change and become a better person
questions.explain: Reformation aims to rehabilitate offenders so they can change and reintegrate into society.

questions.q: Why do some people argue that good intentions can still lead to crime?
options: A person may break the law believing they are doing right, such as stealing to feed a starving child
Intentions have no link to actions
questions.explain: Sometimes people commit crimes from good intentions, like stealing food for a hungry family, raising questions about motive and morality.

questions.q: What does 'retribution' as an aim of punishment mean?
options: The criminal should be set free immediately
The criminal should pay back or suffer for the wrong done
Society should commit the crime too
questions.explain: Retribution is the idea that wrongdoers deserve to be punished in proportion to their crime.

questions.q: What is a 'hate crime'?
options: A crime motivated by prejudice against a person's group or identity
questions.explain: A hate crime is an offence motivated by prejudice, such as racism, religion or sexuality.

questions.q: Which is commonly listed as a cause of crime?
options: Poverty, upbringing and lack of opportunity
questions.explain: Causes of crime often cited include poverty, environment, addiction and lack of opportunity.

questions.q: What does the aim of 'protection' in punishment mean?
options: Keeping society safe by preventing the offender from harming others
questions.explain: Protection means safeguarding the public, for example by imprisoning dangerous offenders.

questions.q: Which describes a non-religious (e.g. Humanist) approach to punishment?
options: Basing it only on holy texts
Focusing on evidence about what reduces harm and helps offenders reform
questions.explain: Humanists tend to favour evidence-based approaches that reduce harm and support reform.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'prison' and 'rehabilitation'?
options: Prison removes freedom; rehabilitation tries to help offenders change
Prison aims only to reward offenders
questions.explain: Prison restricts liberty, while rehabilitation focuses on changing behaviour and reintegrating offenders.

questions.q: Which describes 'community service' as a punishment?
options: Offenders are given a cash reward
Offenders are immediately released without conditions
Offenders carry out unpaid work to benefit the community instead of going to prison
Offenders are sent to a war zone
questions.explain: Community service requires offenders to do unpaid work as a punishment and a way of repaying society.

questions.q: What is meant by the difference between 'evil intentions' and 'evil actions'?
options: They are exactly the same thing
Intentions are what a person plans or wants; actions are what they actually do
questions.explain: Evil intentions are harmful thoughts or plans, while evil actions are the harmful deeds that result.

questions.q: What does 'justice' broadly mean in this topic?
options: Bringing about what is fair and right for victims and offenders
questions.explain: Justice involves fairness - ensuring people receive what they deserve and that wrongs are addressed.

questions.q: Which is a common argument against the death penalty?
options: It guarantees no further crime anywhere
An innocent person could be executed by mistake, and it cannot be undone
It is the cheapest option in every case
questions.explain: A key argument against capital punishment is the irreversible risk of executing an innocent person.

questions.q: Which view best reflects a religious argument against the death penalty?
options: Only God should take life, and offenders may still reform
questions.explain: Many believers oppose capital punishment, arguing life is sacred and offenders may be reformed.

questions.q: Which best reflects a Christian teaching about forgiving those who do wrong?
options: Believers should forgive 'seventy times seven' times
Forgiveness should be given only once
questions.explain: Jesus taught that forgiveness should be limitless ('seventy times seven'), emphasising mercy.
